This is an excellent book. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hare_with_Amber_Eyes

Edmund de Waal is a descendant of the Ephrussi family, which eventually merged with the Rothschilds and who lost the bulk of their fortune in World War 2.

de Waal is an artist and historian and cultural student. His uncle, who served as a Lt. for the US in World War 2, left a collection of 18th century Japanese "Netsuke" objects to de Waal. The book is exploring how the netsuke had been collected and preserved through the generations.

The Ephrussi family came from Czechoslovakia and established a large grain empire. They were Russian Jews, and set up in Paris and Vienna.

The book is a history of that time, those social circles, art collections, trade, politics, and family. When de Waal spends time on the Ephrussi who first collects the netsuke objects, he paints a fair and eventually admirable picture of the man.

When de Waal discusses how his ancestors controlled the entire grain market of many Nations through a monopoly - he doesn't spend more than a few sentences on it. This would seem apropos in keeping with the book's actual focus of the history of the netsuke.

However when the Empire is being dismantled by angry Nazis whose economy had been destroyed, de Waal spends several chapters lamenting how terrible indeed it is that his family had all their toys and castles taken from them.

At no point does the author seem to consider the link between cause and effect. The lack of self-awareness reaches its pinnacle when he is describing their Housekeeper, Anna, who plays a pivotal role in the story of the collection and its safe return.

He laments how his family has lost their estates and how this woman who was their servant for 40 years deserved better than to be separated from her masters. He doesn't put it in as many words, but it is there - a clear insight into the perspective of someone who hasn't really ever understood why his ancestors were so reviled.
The Hare With Amber Eyes - A Slip-On Decoy Book Cover for a Holocaust Memoriam

There is the fundamental difficulty here - you come to care for the Ephrussi family, and especially the children who grow old and pass away through the decades. The uncle Iggie, especially, a Lt. in the Army who seemed to be one of the Monuments Men.

But the book never really discusses in detail the famine caused directly by the Ephrussi family. It glosses over it in a sentence or two before spending a chapter on the downfall of the family's economic fortune.
